title: Demonstratives and possessive determiners
objectives: Choose demonstratives according to number and distance.
Use possessive determiners to show relationships.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: We use this, that, these and those to point to people or things. These words are called demonstratives. This and these often refer to something near the speaker; that and those often refer to something farther away. ‘This chair’ can be a chair next to me, while ‘that chair’ can be across the room. The exact distance depends on the situation.

Use this and that with a singular noun: this book, that book. Use these and those with a plural noun: these books, those books. A demonstrative can also stand alone when the noun is clear: ‘This is mine’ or ‘Those are expensive’.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: A possessive determiner shows a relationship with a person or thing. The forms are my, your, his, her, its, our and their. Put one before a noun: my phone, her brother, our house, their books. The form does not change when the noun is plural: ‘my book’ and ‘my books’.

Choose the determiner from the person who owns or is connected to the thing. ‘Lina has a bicycle. Her bicycle is red.’ ‘Lina and Sam have a bicycle. Their bicycle is red.’ Your can refer to one person or more than one. Its is possessive; it’s is a short form of it is or it has.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Look at the examples below. In a shop, a customer may say ‘How much is this jacket?’ while holding it, and ‘How much are those jackets?’ while pointing across the room. Is agrees with this jacket; are agrees with those jackets. The demonstrative gives information about number and often about position.

Possessive determiners also describe relationships, not only ownership: ‘my sister’, ‘our teacher’ or ‘their city’. His and her refer to the person, not to whether the noun is singular or plural: ‘his sister’, ‘his brothers’, ‘her sister’ and ‘her brothers’ are all possible.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not use this or that with a plural noun in standard English: say ‘these shoes’ or ‘those shoes’. Do not use these or those with a singular countable noun: say ‘this shoe’ or ‘that shoe’. When the noun is uncountable, this and that are also possible: ‘this water’ or ‘that information’.

A possessive determiner needs a following noun: ‘This is my book’. A possessive pronoun can stand alone: ‘This book is mine’. You will study possessive pronouns in the next unit. Remember that its has no apostrophe when it shows possession: ‘The dog is eating its food’.

examples.sentence: This cup in my hand is hot.
examples.note: This points to one nearby cup.

examples.sentence: That building across the road is a library.
examples.note: That points to one building farther away.

examples.sentence: These books beside me are new.
examples.note: These points to nearby plural books.

examples.sentence: Those cars over there are expensive.
examples.note: Those points to plural cars farther away.
My shows a relationship to the speaker.

examples.sentence: The children are doing their homework.
Lena is looking for her keys.
examples.note: Her refers to Lena; keys is plural.

examples.sentence: The dog is eating its food.
examples.note: Its shows the food belongs to the dog.

common_errors.reason: Use these with a plural noun.

common_errors.incorrect: Their house is big. It’s garden is small.
common_errors.correct: Their house is big. Its garden is small.
common_errors.reason: Its is possessive; it’s means it is or it has.

common_errors.incorrect: We live here. Our house are small.
common_errors.correct: We live here. Our house is small.
common_errors.reason: The singular noun house takes is.

summary: Use this and that with singular nouns; use these and those with plural nouns.
This and these often refer to nearby things; that and those often refer to things farther away.
Put possessive determiners such as my, her and their before nouns.
